turns.text: Which brings us back to the colleague arranging interpreters. How does the page describe transactional leadership's effect on fair service and on staff?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: As double-edged, and surprisingly important. On the helpful side, it can turn equity from good intentions into real accountability, by building things like timely accommodations or accessible documents into how performance is measured. And clear, written criteria protect people from vague judgments, such as someone just not feeling like leadership material, which is exactly where bias tends to hide.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: And on the harmful side, I suspect the opening story is the clearest example we could ask for. Measures that quietly punish the people doing the most careful work.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Exactly. If a worker is measured only on calls closed per hour, spending extra time with someone who uses an interpreter or has a cognitive disability makes her numbers look worse. Poorly designed measures can reward unequal service. They can also miss invisible work entirely, such as mentoring newer colleagues or working around tools that are not accessible.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: So what should that supervisor actually do? Telling her to speed up feels wrong, but simply excusing her from the target does not feel quite right either.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Recognize the access work openly, and propose adding it to how the unit measures quality, alongside the count. Clear expectations stay, but now they reward the work that makes the process fair. Access becomes the standard for everyone, rather than one person's extra effort.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: That feels like the real lesson of the style: keep the clarity, but measure the right things. What else does the page recommend for leaders who rely on measures?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Look at every measure and ask whether hitting it encourages people to rush past someone with language, disability or complex needs, and balance speed with quality. Include fair people management and accessibility in how supervisors themselves are evaluated. And pair the measures with purpose, so the team understands why the standards matter to people's dignity and to public trust.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Here is a question to carry with you. What important work on your team does not show up in any measure, and who is doing it? Thank you for listening.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Picture a team that has taken up a new trauma informed approach to working with the public, with real enthusiasm. People are proud of the change. Now another big change is coming, and two of the most committed people on the team seem exhausted.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: That is a good problem and a hard problem at the same time. The team clearly believes in the work. So what does the page mean by transformational leadership?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Transformational leadership connects daily work to a shared purpose, while developing the people who carry it out. Researchers describe four parts. Living the values consistently. Linking routine work to a meaningful future. Encouraging people to question old assumptions without fear of blame. And treating each person as an individual, with coaching and stretch opportunities that fit them.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: That sounds close to charismatic leadership, which also inspires people. What makes the two different from each other?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: The center of gravity. Charismatic leadership centers on the leader. Transformational leadership centers on the shared mission and the growth of the people doing the work. Rather than creating dependence on one person, it deliberately builds other leaders, so the organization gets stronger over time.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: What would I notice day to day with a transformational leader? I am curious how purpose shows up in an ordinary week, not only in big announcements.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Their calendar and budget match what they say matters. They regularly ask whether a process still serves people well, or whether it continues out of habit, and they reward honest critique. Updates connect to real human impact. They invest time in mentoring and in building depth for the future. And they set high expectations paired with real support.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: Where does this style do its best work? It sounds especially suited to moments of big change.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: It is one of the most consistently supported styles for long term effectiveness. It helps during major shifts, such as moving from rule bound, siloed work to service that is centered on the person. By combining clear purpose with individual coaching, it builds motivation that comes from within, so teams solve problems even when no one is watching.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: Which brings us back to those two exhausted colleagues. Where does the page say this style tends to struggle?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Overextension. Leaders drawn to vision and constant improvement can overlook the steady basics: realistic workloads, clear procedures, routine checks. When transformation becomes a permanent state of urgency, even deeply committed people burn out. And in agencies that have lived through several rebrands that changed nothing, a new transformation can meet real cynicism.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: Let's turn to fair service. The page calls transformational leadership a strong platform for equity, but it also names one blind spot. What is it?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: First the strengths. Because these leaders connect work to purpose, staff come to see accessibility and fair service as part of doing excellent work, not as a checklist. Inviting people to question old habits opens the door to rethinking hiring practices, credential rules, inaccessible forms and meeting norms. And individual coaching, offered fairly, helps build a more diverse group of future leaders.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: And the blind spot? I suspect it has something to do with that phrase, we are all one team, which can sound wonderful and still hide something important.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Exactly. This style focuses on improving the organization, not automatically on examining who holds power. A unifying vision can unintentionally paper over real differences in outcomes by race, disability or income. And individual attention can drift toward people who share the leader's background or communication style, widening gaps while the leader believes they are developing everyone.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: So what should the leader in our opening story do about the next change, with two committed people already worn down?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Talk openly about pace. Ask the team what they need to finish the current work well, and stage the new change so no one carries both at once. The purpose stays, and people are protected. Another inspiring vision on top of exhaustion would most likely cost the team its most committed members first.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: That is a generous and practical answer. What does the page suggest for leaders who want to use this style well over time?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Ground the vision in real data that shows where outcomes differ in hiring, promotion, retention and service. Track who receives stretch assignments, visibility and mentoring, so development is fair rather than accidental. And pace change sustainably, retiring old work before adding new demands, especially for staff who carry heavy emotional work.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Here is a question to carry with you. Who on your team is carrying the most change right now, and do they know you see it? Thank you for listening.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Imagine new data showing that people whose first language is not English are approved for a support service at much lower rates than everyone else. When the numbers are shared, some managers feel the data is accusing them personally. The room is tense.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: That tension is real, and I think it is one reason hard data sometimes stays in a drawer. So what kind of leadership does the page describe for a moment like this one?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Transformative leadership, also called equity centered leadership. It examines power and redesigns the systems that produce unequal results, both inside the organization and in the communities it serves. Its starting point is that rules and budgets which look neutral on paper can still produce unequal outcomes, and that those outcomes are design flaws leadership is responsible for fixing.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: The names are confusing, I have to admit. Transformative and transformational sound almost identical. How are they different from each other?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: They are easy to mix up. Transformational leadership focuses on improving performance, innovation and culture. Transformative leadership focuses explicitly on fairness and power. It asks who is being served well, who is not, and why. The scholar Carolyn Shields is closely associated with it.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: What would I notice about a transformative leader in practice? I imagine it is more than speaking up about equity in meetings.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: They look beneath averages. If satisfaction is high overall, they ask who sits in the group that is not being served well, and what barriers they meet. They design programs with the people affected, not only for them. They name barriers plainly, while focusing on redesign rather than blame. Equity priorities show up in real budgets and staffing. And success is measured by smaller gaps, not by the number of trainings held.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: Where is this style most valuable? Public service seems like the obvious answer, but I would love to hear why.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Because in human services, structural patterns shape who gets help and who falls through the cracks. Redesigning the underlying rules, such as eligibility steps, digital accessibility, language access and hiring criteria, produces improvements that outlast any single initiative. The page also mentions the curb cut effect: designing for people facing the most barriers often makes services easier for everyone.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: And yet this is hard work, and it does not always go well. Where does the page say transformative leadership tends to struggle?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Challenging long standing norms creates friction. A leader who relies on urgency alone, without building allies or giving managers practical tools, can become isolated. Redesign takes years, and without visible short term wins people lose patience. There is also a risk of focusing so much on the right words that people freeze, afraid of saying the wrong thing, and practical progress slows.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: The page describes this style as the direct engine of systemic equity. How does it compare with inclusive leadership, which we often hear about in the same breath?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Inclusive leadership shapes whether people feel they belong from day to day. Transformative leadership changes the structures that decide who has access and influence. Together they are powerful. On its own, transformative work moves beyond awareness workshops to concrete changes, such as removing unnecessary degree requirements, redesigning promotion criteria and building accessibility into every public portal from the start.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: You mentioned managers feeling blamed. That seems to be the biggest practical risk for this style. How does the page address it?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Directly. If senior leaders set bold equity expectations without giving supervisors clear tools, realistic workloads and safe places to learn, supervisors feel blamed or overwhelmed, and they become quiet bottlenecks instead of partners. Equipping people is part of the work, not an extra.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: So back to the tense room and the approval data. What would a strong transformative response look like in that meeting?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Share the data as a system problem rather than individual blame, and work with the managers to trace where in the process the gap appears and what to change. That equips them instead of putting them on trial. Holding the data back until it has been studied further would protect comfort while the unequal approvals continue.

turns.speaker: Co-host
turns.text: What else does the page suggest for leaders who want to work this way, especially without burning out themselves or the people around them?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Translate equity into concrete tools: plain language guides, structured interview questions and accessibility checklists. Celebrate practical wins, like faster accommodations or simpler intake forms, to build momentum. And anchor equity goals in strategic plans, budgets and leadership evaluations, so the work belongs to the institution and not to one champion.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Here is a question to carry with you. When you name an unfair result, do people walk away equipped, or blamed? Thank you for listening.
